*   **City Accounting Findings:** City accounting officially logged a "civic gap," and **no formal civic initiative currently on the books answers it** [6, 34–35].

Downtown's sentiment reading fell to **0.41** (8th out of 22 neighborhoods), retail vitality dropped nearly three full points to **9.55**, and housing pressure jumped to **3** (worse than 18 of 22 neighborhoods) [12, 13]. 
*   **Field Testimony & Absence of Ownership:** Caseworker **Merkin Jumper** (holding a folder outside SpeedyBurger) expressed a "wish" for dedicated initiatives [12, 14], while faith leader **Eunice Marston** (Telegraph Presbyterian) confirmed seeing no significant initiatives to address decay as her congregation streams past SpeedyBurger [12, 15]. Caldera explicitly confirmed **no matching program, task force, or municipal office is assigned to manage Downtown's decline** [12, 13, 16].
*   **OARI & East Oakland Response Deficits:** The **Oakland Alternative Response Initiative (OARI)** operates unarmed two-person teams across West Oakland, Fruitvale, and East Oakland [12]. However, telemetry software (**Civis Systems**) flagged negative safety indicators across OARI zones [12]. Crucially, the underlying audit confirmed **there is no prior comparison or baseline history available in the system**—meaning the tool is alarming without historical data to evaluate against [12].

Downtown metrics show multi-metric decline (sentiment 0.41, retail vitality 9.55, housing pressure 3) with zero assigned municipal mitigation programs [12, 13]. OARI lacks published response-time metrics or baseline comparison history in its Civis audit [12].

Y2C106 was that kind of week. The gray hasn't lifted — Noah Tan reported from Lake Merritt on a third consecutive week of overcast skies that have done something to the social fabric of that neighborhood, and it's not a small thing. Toby Lamont told Noah he felt the whole rhythm change. Mina Linas, who monitors the lake and sees who stops and who keeps walking, said even the regulars just nod now and move on. A city under low clouds is still a city, but it operates differently — more interior, more private, more provisional. The benches stay empty. People are waiting for something to break, as Tobi Sobi put it from her kitchen table, watching her kids lose enthusiasm for the outside world.

THE WEEK'S REPORTING By Noah Tan | Bay Tribune Civic Toby Lamont paused at the edge of Lake Merritt, hands deep in his coat pockets, watching the water ripple under the low gray sky. He’d been fighting off a head cold all week, and the damp chill in the air wasn’t helping. “You know, when that gray just sits over Lake Merritt for days,” he said, “it's like the whole rhythm changes.” The usual joggers and walkers were still out, but they moved with purpose—heads down, bundled against the cold, fewer stops to chat. The benches near the water, usually dotted with folks lingering over coffee or conversation, were mostly empty. Mina Linas, who works at the lake’s monitoring station, echoed the sentiment: “I see it at the monitoring station—fewer people stopping to chat, more heads down, quick steps. Even the regulars who usually linger by the water just give me a nod and keep moving.”

THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C107 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C107 There is a particular quality to a city holding its breath, and Oakland has been doing that all week. I don't mean it metaphorically — I mean Lonzo Jailon standing at the edge of Lake Merritt with his clipboard tucked under his arm, rubbing warmth back into his hands because three straight days of rain had given way to a marine layer thick enough to blur the numbered posts he depends on for measurement. As Noah Tan reported it, even the gulls went quiet. That image has stayed with me. A man whose job is precision, standing in the fog, waiting. That is the week's true weather report, and it applies to more than the lake.

============================================================ By Noah Tan | Bay Tribune Civic The Breath Before the Step Lonzo Jailon's fingers hover over the lake markers, tentative in the fog. His usual morning routine—checking the water levels along Lake Merritt's edge—has slowed to a methodical shuffle. The numbered posts he relies on blur into the gray, forcing him to pause, squint, double-check. "That fog rolls in and suddenly the whole lake feels like it's holding its breath," Jailon says, tucking his clipboard under his arm to rub warmth back into his hands. His role as a sea level monitor means trusting measurements, but three straight days of rain followed by this thick marine layer have left even the gulls quiet. "Been keeping to myself more than usual, just... waiting for some sunlight to punch through."

What I keep returning to is Mina Linas showing up twice in this week's reporting. Noah finds her at the monitoring station, watching people withdraw. Kai Marston finds her later at Lakeside Whisper Bar, where she says the place lets you actually hear yourself think. Same person, same week, two environments. The quiet around the lake that reads as social retreat is also, at the right bar on the right night, something closer to intimacy. That's not a contradiction I want to smooth over. It's the same gray weather producing two different human responses depending on whether you have somewhere warm to go.

Trevor Shimizu caught the same stillness at 12th Street Station, where bus driver Coen Cartier described pulling to the curb in the early fog and watching riders linger rather than board, as if the city were pausing before committing to its own momentum. Station worker Eleanor Rivera told Shimizu that fog, holidays, big votes, big games — they all alter the human flow in ways that can't be reduced to a single cause. What I find worth sitting with is that both Cartier and Rivera are essentially describing the same thing Jailon described at the lake: the way external conditions force people to slow down, look harder, and read what's actually in front of them rather than what they expect to find. A bus driver, a monitor, a station worker — none of them in the same story, but all narrating the same week.

Luis heard something similar from Elio Perez — the same Elio who was enthusiastic about the Oaks in Talia's piece — who told him the council talks about accountability but he doesn't see it closing the gap. Depak Ying in Rockridge had heard the same thing secondhand from people he doesn't know, the way these feelings move between people doing the same shift in different zip codes. Luis was careful, and I respect the carefulness: he named the gap but declined to invent a name to put pressure on, because he doesn't have one yet. That's honest reporting. It also means we're sitting with a civic gap that the city's own instruments have flagged, no initiative on the books to answer it, and no office we can point to and ask why.

============================================================ By Luis Navarro | Bay Tribune Civic Council Talk, Neighborhood Math Elio Perez has the rag out before the lunch rush even starts. West Oakland comes in loud through the kitchen door — dish pit running, someone yelling for extra lemons — and he's wiping the same four-top for the third time because his hands need something to do while he talks. "I feel like the council talks a lot about accountability," he says, setting down a stack of menus, "but I don't see much action that actually closes the gap for people like me and my neighbors."

So the question isn't rhetorical, and it isn't mine to answer for them: if the city can see the gap clearly enough to log it, who exactly is supposed to be the one closing it — and how long does a table full of servers in two different neighborhoods have to keep saying the same sentence before somebody with a title says it back? "I've heard people talking about the council not stepping up," he says, "and it feels like there's a disconnect — like they're not hearing what's happening in the neighborhoods. It's frustrating because we're all just trying to make things work here." Two servers, two neighborhoods, one word showing up in both mouths without either of them coordinating it: disconnect. Here's what I can put on the page and what I can't. What's confirmed: the city's own accounting flagged a civic gap this cycle — a distance between what accountability sounds like from the dais and what it does on the ground. That's not my read of the room. That's the finding itself. And paired with it: no civic initiative currently on the books answers that gap. Not a stalled one. Not a delayed one. None.

What isn't confirmed, and what I'm not going to pretend I know: which office owns that gap. Which councilmember, if any, has been asked and gone quiet. Whether a request went out and got nothing back, or whether nobody's filed the request yet. I don't have a name to put pressure on, and I'm not inventing one to make this piece feel more finished than it is. That's the uncomfortable part of this kind of story. Elio and Depak aren't wrong about what they feel. The gap they're describing is real enough that it shows up in the city's own instruments, not just in their frustration. But feeling a disconnect and being able to point to who's responsible for closing it are two different things, and right now only one of those exists on the record.

That question brushes directly against what Jax Caldera found Downtown, and what Luis Navarro found when he talked to servers in two different neighborhoods about the same civic feeling. Jax stood on those eight or nine downtown blocks where retail vitality fell nearly three points, housing pressure is now worse than eighteen of the city's twenty-two neighborhoods, and the sentiment reading has dropped to 0.41 — above the city median, so nobody gets to call it the worst, but moving in the wrong direction with nothing waiting on the other side to catch it. Eunice Marston, who watches her congregation move past SpeedyBurger every week, said she hasn't seen any significant initiatives to address the concerns. Merkin Jumper, a caseworker who notices things professionally, used the word wish. Not expect. Not demand. Wish.

Wish. That's the word doing the work. Not waiting on. Not was told. Wish — like a birthday candle, not a budget line. Here's what the record actually says, because Jumper's gut and the numbers agree for once: Downtown's sentiment reading dropped four-tenths of a point and now sits at 0.41 — eighth out of twenty-two neighborhoods, technically above the city's own median of 0.36, so don't let anybody tell you this is the worst block in town. It isn't. But retail vitality fell nearly three full points to 9.55, and housing pressure jumped a full point to 3, worse than eighteen of twenty-two neighborhoods in this city. Three metrics, three directions, all bad, all landing on the same eight or nine downtown blocks in the same stretch. And when I went looking for the initiative, the task force, the office, the anything with a name on it that's supposed to be sitting on this fire — there's nothing. No matching program. No mitigator. Nobody's desk.

============================================================ By Jax Caldera | Bay Tribune Civic Downtown, Overcast, Nobody's Name on It Merkin Jumper's been standing outside SpeedyBurger on his lunch break for eleven minutes now, folder under his arm, watching the line move fast like it always does. He's a caseworker. He notices things for a living. "I've seen the way the neighborhood is, you know," he tells me, still watching, "the towers staying lit late and people always rushing to and from places like Telegraph Presbyterian and SpeedyBurger. It feels like there's a lot of activity, but at the same time, I've heard people talking about how Downtown is decaying." He shrugs, folder still under his arm. "As someone who works with the community, I feel like I'm making a difference, but I also wish there were more initiatives to address the issues we're facing."

I found Celeste Moon near the towers that stay lit past when anybody's working in them, and she hadn't heard about any of it. "I haven't really thought about it," she said, "but I did hear Downtown was packed last night. That's all I know." Packed. Lit up. And decaying underneath it — those aren't contradictions, they're the same neighborhood wearing two faces depending which number you trust. Then there's Eunice Marston, who runs faith work out of her building and watches her congregation stream past SpeedyBurger every week like clockwork. "I haven't really seen any significant changes or initiatives that address the concerns about Downtown decay," she told me, "but I do see people from my community, like those coming out of Telegraph Presbyterian, going about their daily lives. As a faith leader, I try to stay focused on the people and their needs, rather than getting caught up in the broader issues." That's a pastor telling me, politely, that the city hasn't given her congregation anything to point at either. She's not chasing the broader issues because nobody handed her a broader issue to chase — just a block getting quietly worse under lit windows.

Three people, three vantage points, same blank space where an answer should be. A caseworker who wishes there were more programs. A singer who heard it was packed and left it there. A pastor keeping her eyes on people because the paperwork isn't giving her anything else to look at. Somebody at City Hall owns a map with Downtown's numbers moving the wrong direction on three separate lines at once. Nobody's initiative owns the fix. So who's supposed to be reading this map, and why hasn't anyone told Merkin Jumper, Eunice Marston, or the rest of us what they're seeing?

What I'm watching next week: whether Jax can get a name attached to the Downtown gap, because Eunice Marston and Merkin Jumper deserve something more answerable than a wish. And whether the civic disconnect Luis documented — two servers, two neighborhoods, one word — starts producing any movement at the dais, or whether it just keeps traveling between people who don't know each other but recognize the same feeling the moment someone says it out loud. ============================================================

“Lately at 12th Street, I’ve noticed the crowds come and go with what’s happening around town,” Cartier says later, between shifts. “When there’s a game or some big vote at City Hall, we get that rush before and after. Other days, especially with the fog rolling in, folks seem to stay put more. It’s not just one thing — it’s how all these pieces fit together that changes who’s waiting at the curb when I pull up.” Inside the station, Eleanor Rivera watches it all unfold from her post near the fare gates. “At 12th Street, we see how everything outside the station affects what happens inside,” Rivera says. “Fog, holidays, even a big game downtown — it all changes the flow. People adjust their routines, and we adjust right along with them. It’s not just about numbers going up or down — it’s about reading the neighborhood’s rhythm and keeping things moving.”

Jerald Jensen, the station janitor, sees the shifts in the patterns of trash left behind. “When the fog rolls in thick like it did last week, or when there’s some big game downtown, I see it in the trash cans,” Jensen says. “Overflowing. More coffee cups, more wrappers, more people rushing through like the place owes them money. And when the Baylight vote happened? Whole different kind of crowd — folks in suits leaving flyers everywhere, talking loud like they own the benches I just cleaned.” Joel Wren, a mechanic with AC Transit, sees the crew keeping the buses running. “Those mechanics and drivers? They’re the ones putting in the long hours to make sure everyone gets where they need to go, rain or shine, game day or not,” Wren says.

What breaks first when the fog lifts? The answer waits with the next tide. Meanwhile Chinatown has been carrying weight that fog doesn't explain. Dr. Lila Mezran's reporting this cycle gave us Yu Zen listening from a hospital bed in Rockridge to nurses talking about neighborhood impacts — "It's not just numbers, it's families, neighbors." That sentence should be pinned above every desk in this building. Mezran also gave us two names that represent the distance between recovery and crisis: Marcus Osei, recently back on his feet, and Maurice Franklin, still hospitalized with severe symptoms. What the reporting doesn't yet answer — and what I want answered — is whether the concentration of illness in Chinatown and East Oakland reflects something structural about care access in high-density neighborhoods, or whether this is seasonal pressure landing where it always lands. That question isn't rhetorical. I'm asking Jordan Velez to look at it from the business side next cycle, because the Temescal picture he drew this week — the tight-knit rhythm of Gridiron Analytics and OakTown Social and Temescal Community Health Center all nodding to each other across three blocks — suggests that neighborhood economic health and community health are not separate ledgers. Director Bobby Chen-Ramirez's health center is downstream of everything Velez described. I want to know what that means when a neighboring district is absorbing disproportionate illness burden.

The A's, of course, broke through the fog in the way only playoff baseball can. Anthony Raines put us in the visiting clubhouse in New York where John Ellis sat with a towel over his shoulders after nine innings, four hits, zero earned runs, nine strikeouts. The A's closed the ALDS with a 4-0 win, and Ellis was not modest about what it meant: "We're here to win, and that performance was a statement." Eric Taveras, whose fourth-inning home run was the offensive signature of the night, told Raines that when your pitcher brings that kind of fire, the rest of the roster has no choice but to match it. Back in Fruitvale, Rick Walker and Rafael Pilgrim heard it on the radio and said the same thing independently — this team might have the pitching depth to go somewhere real. The question Raines left open is whether Ellis was a harbinger or an outlier. The ALCS will answer it, and I expect that answer to reverberate through every neighborhood in this city.

Taveras’ home run, his second of the series, was a solo shot in the fourth inning, part of a night where he went one-for-four with one RBI. It wasn’t a barrage of offense, but it didn’t need to be. Ellis’ performance rendered every run a luxury, not a necessity. Back in Oakland, the buzz was palpable. Rick Walker, tuning in from Fruitvale, caught the game on the radio. "I heard about John Ellis' shutout on the radio this morning—what a performance!" he said. "It’s got me thinking the A’s might just have the pitching depth to make a serious playoff run this year." Rafael Pilgrim echoed the sentiment: "I heard about John Ellis' shutout—nine innings, no runs. It’s got people here in Fruitvale buzzing, thinking the A’s might just have the pitching depth to go deep in the playoffs."

The Oaks came up twice too, and in ways that don't quite match. Talia Finch went to West Oakland and found Elio Perez and Daniel Cloak and Darius Clark all saying, with genuine warmth, that the team is reaching toward the community and that it matters. Then Simon Leary spent his week with the A's record — 127-35, a machine more than a team by now — and asked the harder question: at what point does the architecture become the story, rather than the people passing through? Martin Richards, a veteran who knows something about being moved across positions and cities, told Simon that value shifts sometimes overnight. Ollie Campbell, who doesn't even follow sports closely, noticed people talking about how the A's keep winning no matter who's holding the beams. The Oaks engagement Talia documented and the A's apparatus Simon examined are two different models of what a sports franchise can be in this city. One is still trying to be recognized by its neighborhood. The other has achieved something so structural it barely needs anyone's recognition.

Outside, the A’s were winning again. They always were. 127-35, another number in a season of numbers. What does it mean when a machine—and make no mistake, that’s what this is now, not a team but an apparatus—keeps running no matter which gears are swapped out? How does a structure like that bear its own weight? Richards, who has no answers because no one does, only the numbers, squinted at the light through the blinds. “It’s not just about adapting—it’s about understanding that your value shifts, sometimes overnight.”

Down the road, somewhere an engine wasn’t running, Ollie Campbell considered it all from a distance. “I don’t follow sports much,” they admitted, “but I’ve heard folks around here talking about how the A’s keep winning even as players come and go.” They paused, weighing something in their palm. “It’s interesting how they manage to stay strong like that.” Interesting, yes. But what is strength when there’s no alternative? When the structure is designed to stand regardless of who’s holding up the beams? The record doesn’t remember the moments of doubt, the fractures. It only knows the final weight, distributed across whatever—whoever—was available to bear it at the time.

The next day, I met up with Travis Coles, the A's starting pitcher, at a coffee shop in Downtown. "I've felt the city's energy shift with our recent wins," Travis said, his eyes lighting up with excitement. "It's like the whole community is coming together and feeding off our momentum. As a player, it's an incredible feeling to know that our performance is having a direct impact on the people around us." As I walked out of the coffee shop, I ran into Clark Saryan, the Closing Pitcher for the Las Vegas Aviators. "I've seen how a win like that can bring the community together," Clark said, smiling. "It's like a spark that ignites a sense of pride and belonging. As someone who's been around the game, I know how it feels to be part of a team that's on a roll, and I think that energy is infectious. It's not just about the game itself, but about the way it makes people feel - like they're part of something bigger than themselves."

Later that day, I met up with Vladimir Gonzalez, the A's right fielder, at a park in Fruitvale. "It's been amazing to see how the community has come together after our win," Vladimir said, shaking his head in amazement. "I feel like it's brought a lot of energy and excitement to the neighborhood. As a player, it's great to see how our performance can impact the people around us." As I watched the A's take on the Yankees, I couldn't help but feel a sense of pride and excitement. The team's win had brought the community together, and it was clear that the energy was infectious. But as the series continued, I couldn't help but wonder - can the A's keep up the momentum, and what does it mean for the city's sense of identity?

The Oakland Oaks don't yet have a game on their record — preseason zero and zero — but Talia Finch and Selena Grant both found the same energy building in Downtown, the same strangers gathered around bar televisions, the same residents using the word "buzz." Head Coach Wilson Shepard told Finch the city is going to be caught off guard. Adash Stanley, the Oaks' point guard, described the whole city waking up with the team. I'll be honest: I've heard opening-season optimism before, and it doesn't always survive contact with a real schedule. What I'm watching is whether the Oaks can hold community attention in the same week the A's are deep in an ALCS. Oakland is not a city that typically has to divide its sports loyalty in October. This is new territory, and the neighborhoods will feel the split.

As I continued my stroll through Downtown, I caught up with Wilson Shepard, the Head Coach of the Oakland Oaks, who was meeting with the media to address his excitement for the season. "I've been feeling the energy around Downtown, and I think our fans are really excited for the upcoming season. As the Head Coach of the Oakland Oaks, I'm eager to show the city what we're capable of, and I feel like we're going to catch people off guard this year," he said, his voice filled with confidence. Dillon Trevor, a local resident, overheard our conversation and chimed in, "I can feel the energy around Downtown, people are really hyped about The Oaks' upcoming season. As someone who's always out in the neighborhood, I've seen how excited the fans are, and it's infectious. I'm looking forward to seeing what the season brings."

I walked further down Broadway, taking in the sights and sounds of the bustling neighborhood. The smell of freshly brewed coffee wafted through the air, mingling with the chatter of pedestrians. As I turned a corner, I stumbled upon a small, unnamed bar, its doors open to the street. Inside, a group of strangers were gathered around the TV, watching a replay of the Oaks' preseason game. One of them, a young man with a fervent glint in his eye, turned to me and said, "I've felt the excitement building around the Oaks, it's like the whole city is waking up with the team. There's a buzz in the air, and I think people are really looking forward to seeing what they can do this season." I later found out that he was echoing the sentiments of Adash Stanley, the Oaks' point guard, who had said, "I've felt the excitement building around the Oaks, it's like the whole city is waking up with the team. There's a buzz in the air, and I think people are really looking forward to seeing what they can do this season."

The question now is whether Ellis’ performance is a harbinger of things to come or a statistical outlier. His nine strikeouts against zero walks suggest command, and the four hits allowed—all singles—indicate he kept the Yankees’ power in check. But postseason baseball is a game of small samples, and one dominant outing doesn’t guarantee a repeat. The ALCS will test whether Ellis has turned a corner or simply authored a singular masterpiece. For now, the A’s will ride the momentum. Ellis set the tone, Taveras provided just enough offense, and the team heads to the ALCS with confidence. But whether this is the start of a deeper run or a fleeting peak remains to be seen. The board speaks clearly for this game, but the ledger for the series is still unwritten.

Elliot Graye gave us something quieter this week — folding chairs at the Lake Merritt Mindfulness Sangha, gray cushions on the floor, incense faint in the air. Eunice Marston of Telegraph Presbyterian noted that Downtown's faith spaces share a purpose without necessarily sharing an address. Tao Lee's observation — that openings matter precisely when they're not compelled by crisis — is the kind of sentence I want to keep. The fog week, the illness in Chinatown, the playoff electricity: a city under pressure needs places that simply stay open without requiring anything.

At the Telegraph Presbyterian Fellowship, just blocks away, chairs were arranged in concentric circles for evening discussions. Eunice Marston of Telegraph Presbyterian noted the shared purpose among Downtown's spiritual centers. "I haven't had any direct involvement with the Lake Merritt Mindfulness Sangha," she said, "but as a faith leader in Downtown, I appreciate the various initiatives and organizations that bring people together and foster a sense of community."

The Lake Merritt Mindfulness Sangha, founded in 2007, maintains its Downtown storefront as a space where residents can practice without agenda or expectation. Tao Lee, who helps coordinate the space, observed that such openings matter precisely when they're not compelled by crisis. "To be honest, I haven't really thought about the Lake Merritt Mindfulness Sangha that much," Lee said, "but I do know that our neighborhood has a strong sense of community, and it's great to see places like the Telegraph Presbyterian Fellowship opening their doors for support."

============================================================ By Mason Ortega | Bay Tribune Culture The Rhythm Between the Grill and the Mic In the back kitchen of Harborline Grill, Tomas Renteria flips a salmon fillet with the same practiced motion he might use to adjust a microphone level. The podcast host and line cook moves through his Wednesday dinner rush in a rhythm that seems to split his attention perfectly between sizzling protein plates and the stories he collects about this Jack London square neighborhood.

The duality shows in the details—how Renteria's podcast notes sometimes appear between prep lists on the stainless steel counter, how the regulars at the bar seem to lean in when he emerges from the kitchen, still in his apron, to record a quick vox pop during his smoke break. But the real crossover happens after close, when Renteria’s colleagues become his first audience, their off-shift beers turning into impromptu focus groups. They're the ones who remind him that both jobs—feeding bodies and feeding minds—come down to the same question: Did you leave them satisfied?

"Tomas? Yeah, he's got this energy about him—like he's always working on something bigger, even when he's just plating up orders," says Le during a rare lull, wiping her knife down. "You can tell he's listening, not just waiting for his turn to speak." Hill offers a different take between loading sheet trays into the washer: "Man keeps his head down on the line, does his job. I hear the podcast chatter sometimes when we're breaking down stations, but Harborline's not the kind of place where you bring that energy to work. We're all just trying to get through the rush."
